hero.name: Shreya
hero.who: an HR recruiter in Chennai who hires on gut feeling and keeps getting surprised

story.b: Shreya interviews twenty candidates a week for a growing logistics company in Chennai. She is proud of her gut. Within two minutes she usually knows. Last year her gut picked a quiet woman everyone else had rejected, and she became the best team lead in the office. This year it picked a confident man who talked beautifully, and he quit after six weeks, leaving a pile of unchecked invoices. Her manager asks how she decides. Shreya opens her mouth and realises she cannot fully explain. Sometimes her instant reads are brilliant. Sometimes they are badly wrong. Sitting in the office canteen with a filter coffee, she wonders how to tell the difference before it is too late.

ask.q: Shreya's gut has been both brilliant and badly wrong. What is the most useful question for her to explore?
o: Whether to stop trusting her gut completely and use only written tests
When her quick judgments are reliable and when she should slow down
How to decide even faster so she can interview more people
ask.why: Throwing out instinct wastes the times it was right, and going faster only multiplies the mistakes. Her gut is neither magic nor useless. Learning when quick reads tend to work, and when they need a second look, lets her keep the good calls and catch the bad ones.

chapters.take: Quick judgments can be brilliant or badly wrong. The skill is knowing which.

story.b: Shreya decides to study her own first impressions. In a small notebook she writes her two-minute read of every candidate before the full interview, then checks it weeks later against their tests and references. Over a month, a pattern appears. For roles she knows well, like warehouse supervisors, her early reads are surprisingly accurate. Within moments she can tell who has really managed a night shift, from the way they talk about a late truck or a missing loader. One morning she walks past the loading bay at the Ambattur warehouse and senses at once that the team is unhappy. A quick chat with the workers confirms it. Their rest room fan has been broken for a month.

ask.q: Shreya's junior Malar says first impressions are always unfair and should be ignored. What is the best reply?
o: Quick reads can be surprisingly accurate, so note them and check them later
Agree, and ignore all first impressions in every interview from now on
Trust first impressions over any later evidence, since they come first
ask.why: Our minds can pick up real patterns from small slices of information, so ignoring every first read wastes useful signals. Treating them as final is risky too. Writing them down and checking them against later evidence shows where they can be trusted.

chapters.take: Small slices of information can tell you a lot, if you check them later.

story.b: During an interview for an accounts executive, Shreya feels a small knot in her stomach. The candidate is polite, qualified and well dressed. Nothing is obviously wrong. In the past she would either ignore the feeling or reject him without a reason. This time she pauses and asks herself what her mind might have noticed. Replaying the conversation, she spots it. Each time she asked about his last manager, he changed the subject to the company's clients. She asks one more direct question, gently. He admits he left after a dispute over missing payments, and the matter is still open. Shreya thanks him and notes it for the hiring panel. Her gut had seen the pattern before she could name it.

ask.q: In a vendor meeting, Shreya's colleague feels something is off but cannot say why. What should he do?
o: Ignore it, since a feeling without a clear reason means nothing
Cancel the deal at once, because the gut is always right
Pause, ask what his gut might have picked up, then check the facts
ask.why: Fast background thinking often notices patterns before we can explain them, so dismissing the feeling may ignore a real signal. Acting on it blindly is risky too. Pausing to find what triggered it, then checking the facts, gets the best of both.

chapters.take: When your gut flags something, ask what it noticed, then check.

story.b: A candidate named Murugan walks in for a team lead role. He wears a faded shirt, speaks English slowly with long pauses, and studied in a Tamil-medium school near Madurai. Within seconds Shreya feels unimpressed. Then she catches herself and asks what exactly she is judging. His accent? His shirt? Neither says anything about leading a warehouse team. So she asks the same five practical questions she asks everyone, about a delayed shipment, a fight between workers and a missed target, and scores each answer on a simple sheet. Murugan's answers are the most practical she has heard all month. When she switches to Tamil for one question, he lights up and explains a clever fix for night-shift delays. He gets the job.

ask.q: Malar likes a candidate because he is smooth-talking, smartly dressed and from a famous college. What should Shreya advise?
o: Trust that polish and a big college name usually mean strong performance
Score him on the same job questions as everyone, setting aside looks and labels
Hire him quickly before another company snaps him up
ask.why: Polish, clothes and a famous college often trigger a quick good feeling, but they say little about doing the job. Rushing only locks in the bias. Asking everyone the same job-related questions and scoring the answers keeps the decision on what actually matters.

chapters.take: Fast judgments soak up bias. Catch the ones based on looks, accents or labels.

story.b: For a senior warehouse manager role, Shreya's team builds a giant comparison sheet. Twenty-eight columns per candidate: test scores, hobbies, personality labels, typing speed, notice period, social media activity and more. The panel meeting runs for three hours and ends in confusion, with each person defending a different column. That evening, over a plate of bajji at home, Shreya asks herself what truly predicts success in this job. She lists only three things: experience running a large shift, a clean safety record, and how people who worked under them describe them. The next morning she brings a one-page sheet with just those three. The panel agrees on a candidate in forty minutes, and nobody leaves with a headache.

ask.q: Shreya is choosing a flat in Velachery and has compared fifteen listings on thirty details. She feels stuck. What should she do?
o: Pick the three factors that matter most to her and decide on those
Add even more details to the sheet so nothing important is missed
Keep visiting new flats until one of them feels perfect
ask.why: Piling on details often buries the few things that truly matter, and searching for perfect can go on forever. Choosing her top three, maybe rent, commute and water supply, cuts through the noise. Sometimes a better decision comes from knowing what to ignore.

chapters.take: More information is not always better. Know which few things truly matter.

story.b: In December, the company suddenly needs fifteen drivers and loaders before the Pongal rush. Shreya interviews back to back, eats lunch at her desk, and her phone never stops buzzing. By Wednesday she notices her reads are getting sloppy. She has nearly hired a man who did not even have a valid licence. So she changes the conditions. She adds a ten-minute gap between interviews, keeps her phone in a drawer, and asks a senior warehouse supervisor to sit in, someone who has watched hundreds of loaders at work. She also keeps checking her notebook every Friday against how each hire is doing. Her quick judgments, she realises, get better with practice and calm, not with speed.

ask.q: Malar is rushing through interviews under pressure and making shaky calls. What would help her instincts most?
o: Speed up even more, since experience will fix the mistakes
Rely on a long checklist and stop using judgment at all
Slow down slightly, cut distractions and keep checking her calls against results
ask.why: Under heavy pressure, people stop reading situations well, so speeding up adds errors. Dropping judgment entirely throws away a useful skill. A little more time, fewer distractions and regular checks of past calls let her instincts grow sharper and more reliable.

chapters.take: Good instincts grow from experience, calm and honest feedback.

story.b: After Pongal, the warehouse is fully staffed, and Shreya's manager asks again how she decides. This time she has an answer. She still notices her first impression, and writes it down. When something feels off, she asks what she noticed. She watches for looks, accents and big college names before they sway her. She decides on a few factors that matter, not twenty-eight. And she keeps her phone in the drawer during interviews. Murugan now runs the night shift, and his team has the fewest absences in the company. Malar has started her own notebook of first reads. Shreya still trusts her gut, but now she knows when to give it a second look.

chapters.take: Trust your instincts where you have experience, and slow down where bias can creep in.
